life_summary: Adam Samuel Bennion was born on December 2, 1886, in Taylorsville, Utah Territory. He grew up in the Salt Lake Valley during a period of significant Church development and community building. Bennion pursued advanced education and became deeply involved in religious instruction and education. He married Minerva Richards Young, and together they had three sons and two daughters. Before his prominent Church appointment, Bennion established himself as an educational leader and author of religious instruction materials. His publications, including Principles of Teaching (1921) and What It Means to Be a Mormon (1917), reflected his commitment to developing both pedagogical methods and doctrinal clarity. His life embodied the integration of intellectual rigor with spiritual conviction.
church_summary: Bennion served as superintendent of LDS Church Schools and played a central role in expanding the seminary program, which provided religious instruction to youth throughout the Church. He authored extensively on religious principles and trained seminary teachers in effective pedagogical methods. On April 9, 1953, he was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles by President David O. McKay. Despite his call coming late in his life, Bennion served with energy and dedication until his death on February 11, 1958, roughly five years after his ordination as an apostle. His tenure was brief but meaningful, bringing decades of educational expertise to the apostolic office.
